sub_themes.sub_theme: class size effects via enrolment-cap RD

insights.claim: Using rule-predicted class size as the instrument handles fuzzy compliance and scales the first stage across multiple cutoffs.
Enrolment bunches just below the cap, more in budget-constrained schools, and a donut RD may discard the most informative observations.
Strong compliance only at the first cutoff means the estimate speaks to small rural schools, not large urban ones.
Restricting to non-bunching schools is only descriptive because bunching is a school-level behaviour correlated with other traits.
Mechanism evidence within RD should estimate effects on mediators directly rather than decompose effects under extra assumptions.
Smaller classes may improve teacher retention, a longer-run channel that administrative turnover data could measure.
The Jones polynomial's blindness to mutation resembles an estimator invariant to a transformation that cannot identify a parameter.
Classrooms switching to equal-area maps could identify whether Mercator exposure distorts perceived country sizes.
Surface code overhead is a trade of poor encoding rate for easily built nearest-neighbour connectivity.
Published training emissions figures are incomparable without meta-analysis-style harmonisation of hardware, overhead and grid assumptions.
For widely deployed models, inference emissions may matter more than training emissions.
Starter stability arises from acid-driven environmental filtering reset by regular feeding.
Starters from the same flour in different kitchens offer a natural experiment on microbial source contributions.

adjacent_ideas.claim: Class splits that trigger new hires could be exploited to separate retention effects on incumbents from mechanical hiring composition.
Staggered school adoption of equal-area wall maps could support an event-study design on perceived country sizes.
Partial-identification bounds, as used for manipulated running variables, could make AI emissions comparable despite missing location data.
